justification: The article delivers exactly the angle CONTENT_PLAN.md/the task brief promise: one running example (coin change on coins {1,4,5}) carried through every stage -- brute-force recursion (coin-brute), a measured exponential blowup across amounts 10/20/30/40 (coin-blowup, real .NET 10.0.401-on-Windows-11 numbers, call counts multiplying ~3,200x for a 2x amount increase), memoization with a 'find the cache that's never read' bug exercise (coin-memo / coin-memo-buggy), the recursion-depth motivation for tabulation (links out to the recursion article's measured ~19,000-frame ceiling rather than re-deriving it), 2D tabulation with full solution reconstruction (coin-tabulate / Reconstruct), 1D space optimization with a 'prove the two tables agree' exercise that actually runs both across 0..200 (coin-agree), and only then generalizes the identical table shape to LCS and edit distance, each with its own reconstruction (LCS's Reconstruct, edit distance's operation-tracking extend-the-code exercise), closing with a one-paragraph knapsack generalization that deliberately skips a full worked example (documented as intentional in docs/crosslinks/algorithms/dynamic-programming.md). This is a genuine structural differentiator from GeeksforGeeks's coin-change-dp-7 page (fetched: that page solves the *counting* variant, not minimum-coins, and uses a different example per stage) and from Wikipedia's LCS/Edit-distance pages (fetched: both state the recurrence and complexity abstractly with a generic X/Y example, no single example carried through multiple representations, no reconstruction code). I fetched all four cited MS-Learn/NIST sources directly and the article's quotations are verbatim and attached to the sentence they support: Dictionary<TKey,TValue>'s 'close to O(1)... because [it] is implemented as a hash table' matches exactly; NIST DADS's LCS definition ('a maximum length... subsequence of two or more strings') and Levenshtein definition ('the smallest number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to change one string... into another,' with the 1965 Levenshtein paper title) both match exactly, ellipses used honestly. Spot-checking distinctive sentences against GeeksforGeeks and Wikipedia found no verbatim or near-verbatim phrasing -- the article's voice ('the same remaining amount, asked from three different directions,' 'the same table shape, a different question') is its own. No filler: first sentence sets up a concrete scenario and runs code immediately; the closing section ('What makes a problem a dynamic-programming problem') adds new synthesis (the knapsack generalization, the two named CLRS properties tied back to what was just built) rather than restating headings. Headings are specific to content, no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways. Exercises vary in form (find-the-bug, prove-it, extend-the-code), sit mid-article, and keep code/output inside collapsed :::solution::: blocks with no giveaway. Front matter (title 'Dynamic Programming: From Recursion to Tables', description) is accurate and non-clickbait, matching the article's actual content precisely. No NEEDS_MARKUS or placeholder text, no ad code of any kind. Duplication check against the sibling greedy-algorithms.md draft (also currently unreviewed, in a parallel worktree): the two articles' *primary* running examples are properly separated as instructed -- greedy uses {1,3,4}, this article uses {1,4,5} -- and docs/crosslinks/algorithms/dynamic-programming.md documents that separation explicitly as a deliberate boundary. Two concrete issues found; see issues[]. Why not higher: the repeated CLRS chapter-14 citation (see issues[]) is a real, checkable sourcing discrepancy against the sibling article's independently-cited chapter 15, appearing three times (front matter plus two inline citations); until verified/corrected it is a genuine weak-sourcing finding under this rubric, and there is also an unaddressed coincidental overlap with the greedy sibling's own exercise (see issues[]) that a careful policy reviewer reading both articles back-to-back would notice.

issues.location: Front matter `sources[0].title` ('Introduction to Algorithms, 4th ed., chapter 14 (Dynamic Programming)'); body citations near '...states this as one of the two properties...' (overlapping-subproblems paragraph) and '...works through the same problem as a worked example of the general technique' (LCS section)
issues.problem: The article cites CLRS's Dynamic Programming material as chapter 14 in three places (front matter and two inline citations). Dynamic Programming has been chapter 15 in CLRS since at least the 3rd edition (with Greedy Algorithms at chapter 16), and nothing in the 4th edition's earlier chapters (1-14, Foundations/Sorting/Data Structures) was added or removed in a way that would shift Part IV's chapter numbers down by one. The sibling article greedy-algorithms.md, researched independently in a separate worktree, cites the same book as 'chapter 15: Dynamic Programming' and 'chapter 16: Greedy Algorithms' -- a direct disagreement between two sibling articles citing the identical source for the identical topic. I could not reach the publisher's page this session (mitpress.mit.edu returned 403 to automated fetches and the web-search budget was exhausted) to do a final live confirmation, so this needs a primary-source check, but the evidence (unchanged 3rd/4th edition numbering in this range, plus the sibling's independently-sourced chapter 15) points to chapter 14 being wrong here.
issues.fixLooksLike: Re-verify the chapter number for 'Dynamic Programming' in the actual 4th-edition table of contents (a library copy, the publisher's page once reachable, or another primary mirror) and correct all three occurrences (front matter + two inline citations) to match. If chapter 15 is confirmed, also double check no other chapter references in the article need the same correction.

issues.location: Opening section (coins {1,4,5}, amount 8, 'greedy: 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 coins' vs. the true minimum 4+4=2) vs. greedy-algorithms.md's exercise 'Prove it: a second failing system' (same coins {1,4,5}, same amount 8, same greedy result 5+1+1+1=4, same optimal 4+4=2)
issues.problem: This article's crosslinks boundary note correctly documents that its coin set ({1,4,5}) was chosen to differ from greedy-algorithms.md's *primary* running example ({1,3,4}) so the two articles don't share a running example. That separation holds for the primary examples. However, greedy-algorithms.md's own exercise (a collapsed solution, not its main narrative) independently lands on the identical instance -- same coins, same amount, same wrong and right answers -- that this article opens with as its centerpiece. A reader who does both exercises/examples back-to-back would see the exact same worked numbers twice across sibling pages, which is the kind of near-duplicate coverage this rubric flags, even though the overlap looks coincidental (both drafts are in-flight, parallel worktrees) rather than one copying the other.
issues.fixLooksLike: When both articles are next revised, have one of them change the colliding instance -- e.g. greedy's exercise asks about a different amount (or a different coin set entirely) than 8/{1,4,5}, or this article's opening example uses a different amount than 8 -- so no single worked instance appears verbatim in both sibling pages.

issues.location: Closing section, the 0/1 knapsack paragraph ('...fits the same mold without needing its own worked example here...')
issues.problem: Every other technique on the page states its cost explicitly (memoization's O(amount) computed subproblems, the 2D table's O(amount x coins), the 1D table's O(amount) space with a concrete before/after integer count, LCS's stated O(n x m), edit distance's stated Θ(m x n)). The knapsack paragraph gives the recurrence and says it reuses 'the identical row-by-row fill and the identical space-optimization argument' but never states knapsack's own cost (O(items x capacity) time and, before optimization, space), leaving one named algorithm without the explicit cost the editorial brief requires for every algorithm named.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one clause stating knapsack's time/space cost in the same terms as the rest of the page (e.g. 'O(items x capacity) time and space, one-dimensionally reducible the same way').
